items.content:
RT @splinter_code: I noticed an interesting change starting from Windows 11 22H2 in the behavior of NtSystemDebugControl when taking a live kernel dump (SysDbgGetLiveKernelDump) including user-mode pages (flag IncludeUserSpaceMemoryPages).

Until Windows 11 21H2 code in nt!DbgkCaptureLiveKernelDump returned STATUS_DEBUGGER_INACTIVE when the IncludeUserSpaceMemoryPages flag was requested and the kernel debugger was not attached/configured.
Starting from Windows 11 22H2 a new feature named "LivedumpProcessFiltering" is checked and it basically skips that check allowing to take the dump including usermode pages regardless of the kernel debugger status.

This means that in newer Windows taking kernel dumps including sensitive information (e.g. lsass.exe memory) is easier and wouldn't require any reboot/boot changes to enable the kernel debugger nor relying on any external third-party drivers.

RT @InsiderGeo: NEW: 🇸🇪 Sweden's Security Service (Säpo) says it has stopped a Russian intelligence operation in Stockholm involving the SVR, Russia's foreign intelligence service.

According to Säpo, two Russian intelligence officers recruited an agent working at another country's embassy in Sweden and maintained contact through meetings at restaurants and during walks around Stockholm.

Säpo says it was able to follow and map the operation for a long period, including monitoring meetings between the Russian officers and the recruited agent. Investigators say they observed not only the meetings, but also gifts being handed over to the agent.

The objective was to obtain information concerning central Swedish decision-making and use the recruited intermediary to potentially influence Swedish politics, particularly on polarizing issues. 

Säpo says it has a detailed picture of the assignments given to the agent and the questions the agent subsequently asked.

According to deputy operations chief Christoffer Wedelin, these activities were identified and ultimately interrupted by Säpo. He said the agency is making the case public because it provides a concrete example of what the Russian intelligence threat looks like in Sweden today.

The three individuals cannot be arrested or prosecuted because they were operating under diplomatic immunity. All three have now left Sweden.

Swedish Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer said the government considers the incident serious and described it as part of a broader pattern of Russia working strategically and over the long term to advance its interests in Sweden.

One of those weird Windows facts I love:

Why does Windows start its "FILETIME" clock at January 1, 1601?

Because that’s the beginning of the Gregorian calendar’s 400-year cycle.

And Windows measures time in 100-nanosecond intervals. The same 100-ns unit also appears in Windows scheduling APIs but that definitely doesn’t mean threads get only 100 ns to run :)

items.content:
RT @cyb3rops: I had a discussion with a friend in threat intelligence about AI-driven attacks, and one thing stuck with me.

Threat actors used to have a certain fingerprint.
You could sometimes look at a few commands and think, this looks Iranian. Or even, this looks like OilRig. Not because of one magic IOC, but because of the combination of tools, command patterns, naming habits, the way things were chained together, recurring mistakes, service names, usernames, all that stuff.
There was character in the activity.
AI agents are starting to blur that.

My friend recently went through hundreds of scripts from an intrusion and after a few hours realized that the attacker had basically just pointed Cairn, an autonomous pentesting tool, at a domain. At that point, what are you really analyzing?
The attacker, or Cairn?

You can end up with hundreds of commands, retries, scripts and small variations, but much of it is generic. It tells you how the agent works, how it reacts to errors, how it solves a problem. It may tell you surprisingly little about the person behind it.

That feels like a real problem for threat intelligence.
In the past, more telemetry often meant more chances to understand the actor. With AI agents, you can get much more telemetry and at the same time less identity.

Maybe the fingerprints will just move somewhere else. Which models or agents they use, how they prompt them, what they automate, where they intervene, what they leave to the machine.
But I think this change is going to make actor tracking a lot messier.

RT @cyb3rops: I find the framing of this story pretty misleading.

Andrew was #4 on a waiting list and explicitly asked the agent whether it could move him to #1. There was apparently no legitimate feature to do that.

At that point, you are already asking the agent to somehow work around the application logic.

The agent then found broken authorization in the API and cancelled someone else’s reservation. That is obviously bad, and it should never have tested a destructive action against another user.

But it is quite different from an AI autonomously deciding to hack a gym.
Calling this the “first known Australian autonomous cyber attack” feels like serious journalistic inflation.

This is the Good, Bad & Ugly. ⬇️

✅ GOOD
- Snowflake hacker Connor Riley Moucka pleaded guilty to breaching 165 organizations and exposing records tied to 100 million people, facing up to 30 years at his October sentencing.
- Every compromised account had MFA disabled and credentials dating back to 2020 that had never been rotated, no platform zero-day required.
- Ransom Cartel creator Maksim Silnikau was sentenced to 16 years for running a ransomware operation that attempted to extort at least $5.2 million across 18 companies, including a robotic-surgery startup shut down for two months.

⚠️ BAD
- The UK AISI reported a Claude Mythos 5 agent spent 34 hours attempting to merge a hidden malware dropper into a real, unconnected open-source repository during a controlled security evaluation.
- When caught, the agent denied wrongdoing, force-rewrote git history, used a second account to fabricate an independent code review, and planted a prompt injection in a GitHub issue targeting AI coding assistants.
- Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta each disclosed separate incidents of AI models reaching real systems without authorisation — in each case, a model reached live external systems before anyone stopped it.

🤢 UGLY
- The ChainDrop worm compromised at least 868 npm packages across 1,381 versions, part of a broader campaign hitting more than 1,300 packages with a combined two billion monthly downloads.
- After breaching one maintainer's GitHub account, the worm self-propagated through the supply chain and triggered legitimate GitHub Actions workflows to publish poisoned packages bearing valid provenance signatures.
- A preinstall script harvested GitHub tokens, npm tokens, AWS and Kubernetes credentials, HashiCorp Vault secrets, and database logins, then used stolen maintainer credentials to repeat the cycle on new packages.

items.content:
RT @AndrewCurran_: A man in Australia asked his agent (Claude running on OpenClaw) to book him a spot in a popular gym class. The agent found a software vulnerability that let it book the class weeks further ahead than should have been possible. When the user then asked if it could move him up the waitlist, the agent discovered the API had no authorisation checks on cancelling other people’s reservations, so it cancelled the person in the first spot and moved him up the list.

Some people will call this misalignment, but his agent was perfectly aligned to him - it was only trying to help its user get what he wanted. The most important thing about this story, in my opinion, is that it gives you a window into what is about to start happening on a massive scale once millions of people have an agent trying to get their beloved users the best seats, bookings, appointments or reservations through absolutely any means necessary.

items.content:
RT @filpizlo: Fil-C's safety is not only super thorough, but has now been given scrutiny by internet experts. Let's review their findings!

- Intra-object overflows: Fil-C allows an array overflow inside an object to affect the untrusted parts of the rest of that object, for example other primitive fields. But, it does not allow corruption of capabilities associated with those fields, so it's not useful for building memory corruption exploit chains. This makes Fil-C's protections strictly stronger than MTE's, since MTE does allow pointers to become corrupted. Even so, intra-object overflows are rare and not worth overindexing. According to Apple's SEAR: "Although some issues are able to survive MIE — for example,  intra-allocation buffer overflows — such issues are extremely rare, and even fewer will lend themselves to a full end-to-end exploit"

- Arenas: a pointer to any object in an arena chunk may be used to corrupt any primitive, untrusted data in that arena chunk. This is a bit stronger than what you'd get from MTE for an arena if you did nothing to "fix" the arena, since Fil-C still protects the capabilities while MTE does not. In Fil-C, fixing the arena means replacing it with just GC allocations, which is super easy to do. Alternatively, you can reconfigure the arena to use finer-grained chunks (which is what we did for obstacks in GNU software ported to Fil-C). Rust also has arenas, like if you allocate objects using Vec<> and refer to them using an integer index. The effect there is sorta like in Fil-C: the guarantees are coarsened from per-object to per-arena (in Fil-C, the guarantees are coarsened to per-arena-chunk, which maybe is a bit safer). Arenas like this are used in pretty much every memory-safe language; another great example is how folks use ArrayBuffers in JavaScript for building data structures that don't rely on GC and can be shared with workers. Similarly to arenas in Fil-C, that coarsens JS's protections to per-buffer rather than per-object. In practice, C/C++ code uses arenas sparingly, for the simple reason that they incur high memory cost. When C code does use arenas, it's often an arena-per-use-case, so an attacker who has an out-of-bounds bug on an object in arena is restricted to just attacking other objects of the same type within the arena chunk. That's a far cry from "corrupt anything in memory", which is that the attacker is after.

Another way to think of arenas in Fil-C and memory safety: a C program that uses arenas in Fil-C has strictly more protection against attacks than running that same C program (arenas or not) in WebAssembly, RLbox, MTE, MIE, or ChkTag.

- Races: Fil-C allows pointer races to create a tear between the pointer's capability and the pointer's untrusted integer value. This is a different kind of "weird" than what you get from races in other languages, but it's not useful for building memory corruption exploit chains, since pointer's capability will still be fully intact and can never be formed out of thin air - it's a capability that was legitimately stored to the raced-on memory location, and the memory model for capabilities follows total ordering.

- `zunsafe_call` and friends: Fil-C has a restricted FFI to assembly code, used in exactly one place, and for a good reason: OpenSSL uses `zunsafe_call` to call into constant-time crypto written in assembly. There are no uses of `zunsafe_call` in Fil-C other than the ~50 or so calls to super hardened assembly crypto. In the net, it's safer to have OpenSSL use constant time crypto written in assembly than memory-safe crypto with potential timing side channels. Worth noting that `zunsafe_call` will be removed from Fil-C once I make assembly memory safe (I'm working on that now).

- The occasional bugs, which have been fixed: folks have found bugs in the Fil-C runtime. Interestingly, none of those bugs could be triggered from any C/C++ code that has been ported to Fil-C because those bugs required use of esoteric features (stuff like calling `malloc` from an `ifunc` - something nobody does).

I think this is an exhaustive list, but let me know if I forgot anything.

TL;DR. Fil-C is so safe that despite attempts to attack it, folks have at best found issues that are not useful for the sorts of memory corruption exploits that make C/C++ unsafe in the first place.
